title: theglobe.com (1995–2001): the bubble’s record IPO · Spectre Brands
description: theglobe.com offered free home pages and chat, set a first-day record with its 1998 IPO, lost $217M in seven years and shut its community in 2001.

card.blurb: Two Cornell students built a site for free home pages and chat. Its shares rose 606% on their first day of trading in 1998. Less than three years later the site was switched off.

stat.label: first-day gain on November 13, 1998, then a record

hero.dates: Incorporated May 1, 1995. Community site closed Aug 15, 2001.
hero.standfirst: For one Friday in November 1998 it was the most successful stock offering in history. It never made a profit.
hero.deck: theglobe.com was a web community, with free home pages, chat rooms and message boards, that sold advertising against the traffic and shut down in August 2001. Its initial public offering in November 1998 was priced at $9 a share and closed its first day at $63.50, a record gain that came to stand for the [bubble](/category/dotcom/). The company then raised another $65M, bought games sites and a web host, and lost $103.9M in 2000 alone. When the online advertising market fell apart it sold the games sites and became, by 2008, a public company with nothing in it. The sources are its [SEC filings](#sources), which run without a break from 1998 to 2026, and the press of the time.
hero.artCaption: Original illustration of a late-1990s home page on a beige monitor, with a globe and a visitor counter. Not an official asset; the page and the globe are our own drawing.

findings.title: The IPO day was the peak of the story, not the business.
findings.text: The shares closed at $63.50 on the first day, about $31.75 after the 1999 stock split. No quarter afterwards closed higher than $39.47, and by the fourth quarter of 2000 the high was $0.84.[^3][^5][^7]

findings.title: It sold advertising and spent more than it took in.
findings.text: In 2000 revenue was $29.9M. Sales and marketing alone cost $23.9M, and total operating expenses were $115.9M.[^7]

findings.title: It bought growth with its stock.
findings.text: Attitude Network cost $46.8M in 1999, Webjump $13.0M and Chips & Bits $15.3M in 2000, paid largely in shares. In 2000 and 2001 the company wrote off or amortized $94.1M (derived) of goodwill and intangibles and restructuring.[^5][^7][^11]

findings.title: The advertising market decided the end.
findings.text: The company said it closed the community “due to the significant and prolonged decline in the Internet advertising sector.”[^8]
